name: Haifa Bay (Zevulun coast) sediment budget and erosion
year_built: Haifa Port main breakwater 1929-1933 (British Mandate; construction start conflicts with English Wikipedia's 1922); Kishon Port 1951; Bay Port/Carmel Container Terminal breakwater extension (~880 m) completed ~2010s; Kiryat Haim 7-breakwater plan approved Dec 2024, appeals rejected ~Mar 2026, not yet built
closed: not applicable - ongoing erosion problem, mitigation still in planning/approval stage
type: Sediment-budget / coastal-erosion case study, not a single built reef: covers the Haifa Port main breakwater (root cause, unintentional sand trap), Kishon Port breakwaters, the proposed Kiryat Haim 7-breakwater + sand-nourishment mitigation plan, and the academic sediment-budget research (Zviely, Kit, Klein et al.) that quantifies it
purpose: Original breakwater: shelter Israel's only natural Mediterranean harbor for shipping. Modern works: restore beaches eroded as a side-effect (Kiryat Haim, Kiryat Yam)
designer: British Mandate port authorities (1929-1933 breakwater); Israel Ports Company for modern Kiryat Haim/Bay Port works, with CAMERI (Technion, founded 1976) providing physical/numerical coastal modeling
financed_by: Israel Ports Company / Israel Ports Development & Assets Company (modern works); British Mandate government (original port)
outcome_one_liner: The 1929-1933 Haifa Port breakwater sits at the Nile littoral cell's northern terminus and unintentionally trapped ~66,000 m3/yr of sand for 75+ years (peer-reviewed Zviely et al. 2007/2009), starving downdrift beaches; Haifa Bay flipped from ~70,000 m3/yr net accretion (1799-1928) to ~7,000 m3/yr net erosion (1928-2006); Kiryat Haim beaches became critically eroded from ~2011, prompting a 7-breakwater + sand-nourishment plan (approved Dec 2024, appeals rejected Mar 2026, not yet built) opposed by NGOs Zalul and Adam Teva V'Din as outdated; Israel's ~0.3-0.5 m microtidal range (confirmed by a 2024 peer-reviewed tidal study ~50 km offshore Haifa) is far smaller than macro-tidal reef sites elsewhere.
